1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Male patient, 65 years old, from Yinchuan, Ningxia, was admitted on Day 0, with the chief complaint of "intermittent cough accompanied by fatigue and headache for more than 10 days." The patient developed cough and sputum production after catching a chill on Day -10. The sputum was white, mucoid, and scant. The cough was clearly related to inspiration, mostly worse at night, and could be somewhat relieved on waking in the morning. He reported generalized fatigue and pain, dull headache, fever, and other symptoms; measured body temperature was 37.8℃. After self-administering 1 ibuprofen sustained-release capsule, the symptoms were somewhat relieved, and repeat body temperature was normal, but chest tightness and tenderness to pressure at the right anterior 2nd intercostal space developed. There was no obvious sneezing, rhinorrhea, or sore throat; no rash or joint pain; no night sweats; and no discomfort such as palpitations, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, or chest oppression. He self-administered "cough medicine and anti-inflammatory medication" with poor effect. Over the past 10 days, the above symptoms gradually worsened, so he presented to our outpatient clinic. Outpatient chest CT showed: narrowing of the bronchus in the right lower lobe with partial atelectasis of the right lower lobe; enlargement of right hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes; right pleural effusion; bilateral emphysema; linear opacity in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe. Blood routine showed: white blood cell count 13.40×10^9/L↑, lymphocyte percentage 11.0%↓, neutrophil percentage 80.8%↑, monocyte absolute count 0.74×10^9/L↑, neutrophil absolute count 10.81×10^9/L↑, platelet count 400×10^9/L↑, hemoglobin 129g/L↓, CRP 50.34mg/L↑. The patient was previously in good health and had a history of "chronic gastritis" for more than 10 years. He had smoked for 40 years, about 10 cigarettes per day, and has not quit smoking. Physical examination: temperature 36.6℃, pulse 86/min, respiratory rate 21/min, blood pressure 130/85mmHg. Percussion of both lungs was resonant; breath sounds were decreased in the right lower lung, coarse in the right upper lung, and clear in the left lung; no Velcro rales were heard in either lung, and no pleural friction rub was heard. Cardiac and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

stage2_input.text: Laboratory tests after admission: CBC: WBC count 8.00×10^9/L, lymphocyte percentage 15.4%↓, neutrophil percentage 73.2%, eosinophil percentage 5.3%↑, platelet count 375×10^9/L↑, hemoglobin 120g/L↓. Procalcitonin was normal. Biochemical markers: NT-proBNP 227.00pg/ml↑, CRP 15.30mg/L↑, albumin/globulin ratio 1.0↓, albumin 33.6g/L↓, blood urea nitrogen 3.14mmol/L↓, creatinine 45.0umol/L↓, globulin 33.3g/L↑, potassium 3.44mmol/L↓. Coagulation function: fibrinogen 5.640g/L↑, D-dimer (quantitative) 1.477ug/mL↑. Eight infectious disease markers: hepatitis B e antibody quantitative 50.60Inh%↑, hepatitis B core antibody quantitative 11.50C.O.I↑. Fungal GM test and G test (-). Sputum culture showed no pathogenic bacteria. Pulmonary tumor markers: ferritin 434ug/L↑, carbohydrate antigen CA125 69.50U/ml↑. TB-related tests: PPD (-); T-SPOT-TB negative. ECG was roughly normal. Echocardiography: small pericardial effusion, aortic valve calcification, mild tricuspid regurgitation. Abdominal ultrasound: imaging favored hepatic hemangioma and gallbladder polyp. Cervical lymph node ultrasound showed no definite enlargement. Enhanced chest CT on Day +1 showed: partial atelectasis of the right lower lobe, narrowing of the right lower lobe bronchus, enhancement on contrast-enhanced scan, with CT values of approximately 57/52HU in different phases; increased translucency of both lungs; enlarged lymph nodes in the right hilum, right paratracheal region, and subcarinal region, with the largest measuring approximately 3.6cm×2.2cm; arc-shaped fluid-density shadow in the right pleural cavity. Brain MRI on Day +2 and contrast-enhanced MRI on Day +5 suggested lacunar cerebral infarctions with partial malacia formation in the right periventricular region, left lentiform nucleus, bilateral caudate nuclei, and right thalamus; no abnormal enhancement was seen in the brain parenchyma. Bronchoscopy on Day +2 indicated: widening of the intersegmental ridge of the right middle lobe, neoplastic growth in the basal segment of the right lower lobe causing luminal obstruction, with 6 biopsy specimens taken from this site; nodular neoplastic growth at the 7 o’clock position of the orifice of the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe. BALF bacterial culture and fungal culture were both negative, and acid-fast stain was negative. Bronchoscopic pathology result on Day +3 indicated: (basal segment of the right lower lobe) bronchial mucosal tissue with chronic inflammation, inflammatory exudation, and fibrous tissue hyperplasia; partial lymphocyte and plasma cell proliferation was active with compression deformation.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: On Day +6, bronchoscopy with cryobiopsy showed: extrinsic compressive bulging of the lateral wall of the right middle lobe; a neoplasm obstructing the lumen in the basal segment of the right lower lobe with necrotic material adherent to the surface; cryosection and forceps biopsy specimens were sent for pathologic examination. New granulation tissue was visible in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 65-year-old man with a long smoking history. At admission, cough, sputum production, low-grade fever, and fatigue had progressively worsened. Chest CT showed narrowing of the right lower lobe bronchus, partial atelectasis, hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and right pleural effusion. Bronchoscopy further showed a neoplasm in the basal segment of the right lower lobe obstructing the lumen. The primary clinical issue that must first be resolved is whether the obstruction is neoplastic or caused by an infectious/inflammatory granulomatous lesion. Previous routine biopsy showed only chronic inflammation and fibrous tissue hyperplasia, which was not fully consistent with the imaging and bronchoscopic appearance of a 'neoplasm,' and there were problems of superficial sampling, interference from necrotic tissue, and insufficient specimen volume. Cryobiopsy can obtain larger, deeper, and more intact tissue samples, and is especially suitable for characterization of lesions with necrosis, granulomas, and endobronchial obstruction. It may help improve the differential diagnostic yield for lung cancer, bronchial TB, nontuberculous mycobacteria-related granulomatous lesions, and other inflammatory lesions, and provide key histopathologic evidence for subsequent selection of medical anti-infective treatment versus an oncologic treatment pathway.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Cryobiopsy and forceps biopsy specimens were submitted for pathological examination.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The core clinical dilemma in this case is that both imaging and endoscopic findings strongly suggest an occupying lesion: stenosis and obstruction of the right lower lobe bronchus, atelectasis, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, and pleural effusion; moreover, the patient is elderly and has a smoking history. However, infectious markers had also been elevated, and earlier there had been fever, cough, and white sputum, indicating that an infectious lesion also warrants attention. Pathologic examination of the cryobiopsy and forceps biopsy specimens is the most direct and critical method for definitive characterization, and can determine whether there are changes such as malignant tumor, necrotizing inflammation, granulation tissue formation, epithelial atypical hyperplasia, and eosinophilic infiltration, thereby explaining why the lesion appeared as a 'neoplasm' on bronchoscopy. The purpose of this examination is to clarify the nature of the lesion, exclude important differential diagnoses such as lung cancer and TB, identify the degree of inflammatory response and tissue injury, and on this basis decide whether to continue anti-infective treatment and observation with follow-up, or to proceed with further oncologic or surgical evaluation.

recommended_exams.exam: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (gene chip method): 13-item bacterial panel and bacterial species identification
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid: (gene chip method) 13 bacterial targets and species identification: Mycobacterial species identification: suggests M. chelonae/M. abscessus, copy number 1667.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although the patient’s illness began with cough after exposure to cold, low-grade fever, and elevated inflammatory markers, routine sputum culture, BALF bacterial and fungal cultures, and acid-fast staining were all negative, PCT was normal, and the early empiric anti-infective therapy was ineffective, suggesting insufficient evidence for common bacterial infection. Meanwhile, the imaging and microscopic findings could not be explained solely by ordinary pneumonia. BALF gene chip pathogen testing can improve detection of special pathogens, especially mycobacteria-related pathogens, when routine cultures are negative, thereby resolving the key question of ‘tumor or special infection.’ This test is of important value for identifying difficult-to-culture pathogens, narrowing the differential diagnosis among TB, nontuberculous mycobacteria, and other infectious lesions, and reducing the risk of misclassification as tumor based on morphology alone. It also directly affects the direction of subsequent antimicrobial therapy and whether long-term targeted treatment is needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Mycobacterial species identification: suggests Mycobacterium chelonae/abscessus, copy number 1667.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In the context of negative PPD and T-SPOT-TB results, negative acid-fast staining of sputum and lavage fluid, no typical tuberculous granulomas on pathology, and microscopic lesions showing neoplasm-like obstruction with necrosis and a background of granulation tissue formation, simply confirming the presence or absence of mycobacteria is still insufficient to guide diagnosis and treatment; further species identification is the निर्णating step. This is because Mycobacterium tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacteria differ significantly in isolation requirements, treatment drug combinations, treatment duration, and prognostic assessment, while Mycobacterium chelonae/abscessus belongs to the relatively difficult-to-treat rapidly growing mycobacteria in clinical practice. Definitive species identification is of key importance for explaining the patient's endobronchial granuloma-like proliferation, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, and atelectasis. The main clinical purpose of this test is to confirm the nature of the pathogen, exclude pulmonary TB, support the diagnosis of nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease, and provide a basis for subsequent regimen selection such as amikacin, azithromycin, and moxifloxacin.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: The thoracic surgery department in the MDT consultation recommended continuing medical therapy and dynamic follow-up CT.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although the lavage fluid gene chip suggested Mycobacterium chelonae/abscessus, and the pathology was also more suggestive of severe chronic inflammation with necrosis and granulation tissue hyperplasia, the initial imaging and bronchoscopic appearance in this case were highly similar to an occupying lesion, and the pathology still contained components requiring vigilance, such as 'some cells showing highly active proliferation' and 'mild atypical hyperplasia of focal squamous epithelium'; therefore, imaging follow-up cannot be completely discontinued on the basis of a single result alone. The MDT recommended dynamic repeat CT, with the aim of continuously assessing the change trends of the right lower lobe lesion, bronchial obstruction changes, mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes, and pleural effusion, and further verifying whether they gradually resolve with anti-mycobacterial/anti-infective treatment. This examination can monitor treatment response and detect early lesion progression or imaging findings inconsistent with expectations without adding significant invasive risk, thereby determining whether to continue the current medical regimen or whether repeat tissue sampling is needed, with re-evaluation for a neoplastic lesion or adjustment of the treatment strategy.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: On Day +6, bronchoscopy with cryobiopsy showed: extrinsic compressive bulging of the lateral wall of the right middle lobe; a neoplasm obstructing the lumen of the basal segment of the right lower lobe with surface-adherent necrosis; frozen section from cryobiopsy and forceps biopsy specimens were submitted for pathologic examination. Neogranulation tissue was seen in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid: (gene chip method) 13-item bacterial panel with species identification: Mycobacterium species identification suggested M. abscessus/M. chelonae, copy number 1667. Bronchoscopic pathology on Day +8 showed: [biopsy of the basal segment of the right lower lobe] chronic inflammation of the bronchial mucosa with granulation tissue formation. Bronchoscopic pathology result on Day +15: (basal segment of the right lower lobe) severe chronic inflammation of bronchial mucosal tissue with squamous metaplasia of the mucosal epithelium, inflammatory exudation, necrosis, granulation tissue proliferation, and a large number of eosinophil infiltrates; some cells showed highly active proliferation, and focal squamous epithelium showed mild atypical hyperplasia. MDT consultation: thoracic surgery recommended continuing medical treatment and dynamic follow-up with CT. Repeat complete blood count on Day +13: eosinophil percentage 12.3%↑. Repeat chest CT on Day +13: the extent of the right lower lobe lesion was reduced compared with before, and the right pleural effusion was decreased compared with before.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease (right lower, M. chelonae/M. abscessus)
diagnostic_basis: Basic characteristics: elderly male, short duration of onset, no special features in the medical history.
Symptoms: cough, sputum production, and other respiratory symptoms; low-grade fever, fatigue, accompanied by headache and chest pain.
Physical signs: except for decreased breath sounds in the right lower lobe, no other obvious abnormalities.

Ancillary examinations: Chest CT - partial atelectasis of the right lower lobe, narrowing of the right lower lobe bronchus, enhancement on contrast-enhanced scan, CT values of approximately 57/52 HU in each phase; enlarged lymph nodes at the right hilum and right paratracheal and subcarinal regions, the largest measuring approximately 3.6 cm × 2.2 cm; small right pleural effusion. Bronchoscopy - neoplasm at the orifice of the basal segment bronchus of the right lower lobe, causing luminal obstruction and stenosis; nodule in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe. Cryobiopsy pathology - severe chronic inflammation of bronchial mucosal tissue with squamous metaplasia of the mucosal epithelium and inflammatory exudation, necrosis, granulation tissue proliferation, and extensive eosinophilic infiltration; some cells show highly active proliferation; focal mild atypical hyperplasia of the squamous epithelium. Lavage fluid - (gene chip method) 13-item bacterial panel and species identification. Mycobacterial species identification - suggests Mycobacterium chelonae/abscessus, copy number 1667.

treatment_plan: Amikacin injection 700 mg IV drip once daily
Continue treatment with moxifloxacin tablets 0.4 g once daily
treatment_response: The patient had no cough or sputum production, no chest tightness or shortness of breath, and no discomfort such as headache.

Repeat chest CT on Day +30 showed: the extent of the lesion in the right lower lobe was reduced compared with before; the right pleural effusion was essentially absorbed; the mediastinal and right hilar lymph nodes were somewhat smaller than before.

Follow-up chest CT on Day +44 showed that the extent of the lesion in the right lower lobe was slightly smaller than before, the right pleural effusion was essentially absorbed, and there was no significant change in the mediastinal and right hilar lymph nodes compared with before.
